questions.stem: What does 「あのくもはわたあめみたいです。」 mean?
options: That cloud is bigger than fairy floss.
That cloud looks like fairy floss.
That cloud is made of fairy floss.
I would like some fairy floss like that.
questions.explanation: 「Noun + みたいです」 says something resembles the noun: the cloud looks like fairy floss. It is a comparison of appearance, not a claim about what the cloud is made of, and it has nothing to do with wanting (「ほしい」).

questions.stem: What does 「らしい」 tell you in 「あの店のラーメンはおいしいらしいです。」?
options: The speaker has eaten there many times
The speaker is sure it is the best ramen
The speaker is inviting you to go there
The speaker has heard it, not tried it
questions.explanation: 「らしい」 marks information the speaker has gathered from others or from signs, so the sentence means 'Apparently the ramen there is good.' Someone who had eaten it would just say 「おいしいです」.

questions.stem: What does 「弟はゲームばかりしています。」 mean?
options: My younger brother is good at playing games.
My younger brother does nothing but play games.
My younger brother has just started a game.
My younger brother plays games only sometimes.
questions.explanation: 「ばかり」 after a noun means 'nothing but' or 'only ever', and often carries a note of complaint. It is the opposite of doing something only sometimes, and says nothing about skill.

questions.stem: What does 「など」 add to 「スーパーで、パンやたまごなどを買いました。」?
options: It shows the list goes on: bread, eggs and so on
It shows only bread and eggs were bought
It shows the bread and eggs were cheap
It shows the shopping was done quickly
questions.explanation: 「など」 at the end of a list means 'and so on', telling the listener that the items named are examples. It pairs naturally with 「や」, which also suggests an incomplete list; 「と」 would list exactly what was bought.

questions.stem: In a formal essay, which word replaces 「でも」 at the start of a sentence to mean 'however'?
questions.explanation: 「しかし」 is the written, more formal word for 'however', where conversation uses 「でも」. 「それから」 means 'and then', 「だから」 'so' and 「たとえば」 'for example'.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「日本の学校はオーストラリアの学校と ___ ところが多いです。」 ('Japanese schools differ from Australian schools in many ways')?
questions.explanation: A plain verb goes straight before the noun it describes: 「ちがうところ」, 'points that differ'. 「ちがい」 is the noun 'difference', 「ちがって」 is the て-form, and verbs never take 「な」 before a noun.

questions.stem: Which question casually asks a friend whether she likes sushi or ramen more?
options: 「すしとラーメンは、どこが好き？」
「すしとラーメンと、どっちのほうが好き？」
「すしとラーメンと、どれのほうが好き？」
「すしとラーメンと、何のほうが好き？」
questions.explanation: Choosing between two things uses 「どっち」 (casual for 「どちら」) with 「のほうが」. 「どれ」 is for choosing among three or more, 「何のほうが」 is not used for comparisons, and 「どこが好き」 asks what you like about something.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「___ たくさんは食べられません。」 ('I can't eat this much')?
questions.explanation: 「こんなに」 means 'this much' or 'to this extent' and goes before an adjective or quantity, as 「そんなに」 and 「あんなに」 do. 「これに」 means 'to this one', and 「この」 must be followed by a noun.

questions.stem: Your host mother says 「こちらは山田さんです。」 What is she doing?
options: Asking you where Yamada is right now
Telling you that Yamada lives near here
Pointing out the way to Yamada's house
questions.explanation: 「こちら」 is the polite form of 「これ」 and 「ここ」, and 「こちらは〜です」 is the usual way to introduce a person who is with you. Introducing someone as 「これ」 would sound rude.

questions.stem: Which connector introduces an example?
questions.explanation: 「たとえば」 means 'for example' and is followed by a specific case. 「それから」 means 'and then', 「ところで」 changes the subject ('by the way') and 「しかし」 introduces a contrast.

questions.stem: Which ending completes 「私は夏が好きです。なぜなら、海でおよげる ___。」?
questions.explanation: A sentence beginning with 「なぜなら」 ('the reason is') is closed with 「からです」 to round off the explanation. A sentence cannot end on 「ので」, and 「ためです」 or 「ことです」 do not complete the 「なぜなら」 pattern.

questions.stem: What does 「それに」 do in 「この店は安いです。それに、おいしいです。」?
options: Gives the reason for the first point
Shows what happened after the first point
Adds a further point in the same direction
Introduces a contrast with the first point
questions.explanation: 「それに」 means 'what's more' and piles a second point onto the first: the shop is cheap, and on top of that the food is good. A contrast would need 「でも」 or 「しかし」, and a sequence of events 「それから」.

questions.stem: What does 「前から三番目の人」 mean?
options: the third person from the front
the three people at the front
the person who came three days ago
the person in front of number three
questions.explanation: 「番目」 after a number gives order: 「三番目」 is 'the third'. 「前から」 sets the starting point, so it is the third person counting from the front. 'Three people' would be 「三人」.

questions.stem: What does 「弟は中学二年生です。」 mean?
options: My younger brother will start junior high in two years.
My younger brother is in second year of junior high.
My younger brother has been at junior high two years.
My younger brother goes to two junior high schools.
questions.explanation: 「年生」 after a number gives a student's year level, so 「中学二年生」 is a second-year junior high student. It names his current year, not how long he has been there.

questions.stem: What does 「しかたがない」 mean?
options: I don't know how to do it.
questions.explanation: 「しかたがない」 (or casual 「しょうがない」) accepts a situation that cannot be changed: 'It can't be helped.' 「かまいません」 is closer to 'It doesn't matter', and 'I don't know how' would be 「やりかたがわかりません」.

questions.stem: A shop assistant asks if you would like a bag. Which reply politely declines?
questions.explanation: 「だいじょうぶです」 and 「けっこうです」 both politely turn down an offer, with 「いいえ」 making the refusal clear. 「しつれいします」 is said when entering or leaving, and 「どういたしまして」 answers someone's thanks.

questions.stem: What do you say as you enter someone's home?
questions.explanation: A visitor says 「おじゃまします」, literally 'I will be in your way', on entering. 「ただいま」 is said by family members coming home, 「おかえりなさい」 is the reply to it, and 「いってきます」 is said when leaving home.

questions.stem: What does 「どうしたらいいですか。」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「Verb たらいいです」 asks for or gives advice, and with 「どう」 it becomes 'What should I do?' It is the usual way to ask someone for help with a problem.

questions.stem: Your friend has a cold and says she is staying up late. What does 「早くねたらどう？」 do?
options: Suggests she go to bed early
Asks what time she went to bed
Tells her she must go to bed now
questions.explanation: 「Verb たらどう？」 is a casual suggestion: 'Why don't you go to bed early?' It leaves the choice to the listener, unlike an order such as 「ねなさい」.

questions.stem: What does 「来ても来なくてもいいです。」 mean?
options: If you don't come, it's a problem.
It's fine whether you come or not.
You must come, even if you are late.
Even if you come, I won't be here.
questions.explanation: 「〜てもいい」 gives permission and 「〜なくてもいい」 says something is not necessary; put together they mean either choice is fine. Nothing in the sentence obliges the listener to come.

questions.stem: Your friend checks the time and says 「あ、もう帰らなくちゃ。」 What does she mean?
options: I have to go home now.
I don't want to go home yet.
questions.explanation: 「なくちゃ」 is the casual spoken short form of 「なくてはいけない」, with the same meaning as 「なければなりません」: 'I have to go home.' It is common among friends but too casual for formal writing.

questions.stem: What does 「学生はもっと本を読むべきだと思います。」 mean?
options: I think students are able to read more books.
I think students should read more books.
I think students read more books than before.
I think students want to read more books.
questions.explanation: 「Plain verb + べきだ」 states what ought to be done, and 「と思います」 marks it as the speaker's opinion. It is a strong recommendation, not a description of what students already do or want.

questions.stem: How does 「来週、京都に行くよていです。」 differ from 「来週、京都に行くつもりです。」?
options: 「よてい」 is an arranged plan; 「つもり」 is a personal intention
「よてい」 is a wish; 「つもり」 is a firm booking
「よてい」 is past; 「つもり」 is future
「よてい」 is casual; 「つもり」 is formal
questions.explanation: 「よてい」 means a schedule or arrangement, such as a booked trip, while 「つもり」 states what the speaker intends to do. Both look to the future and both can be used politely.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「田中さんは今日休みだから、家にいる ___ です。」 ('Tanaka has the day off, so he should be at home')?
questions.explanation: 「はず」 gives what the speaker expects to be true from the facts: he has the day off, so he should be at home. 「つもり」 and 「よてい」 describe plans, which the speaker cannot make on Tanaka's behalf.

questions.stem: Which ending completes 「明日は雨がふる ___。」 ('It might rain tomorrow')?
questions.explanation: 「かもしれません」 after a plain form expresses possibility: 'it might rain'. 「つもりです」 states a person's intention, which rain cannot have, and the other endings do not express likelihood at all.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「ねる ___、はをみがきます。」 ('I brush my teeth before I go to bed')?
questions.explanation: 「Plain non-past verb + 前に」 means 'before doing'. 「後で」 needs the た-form (「ねた後で」), 「ながら」 needs the ます-stem, and 「てから」 attaches only to a て-form, so none of them fits after 「ねる」.

questions.stem: What does 「明日のパーティーに行けるかどうか、まだわかりません。」 mean?
options: I don't know yet where tomorrow's party will be held.
I don't know yet who is going to the party tomorrow.
I don't know yet what time the party starts tomorrow.
I don't know yet whether I can go to the party tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 「〜かどうか」 means 'whether or not', so the speaker is unsure whether she will be able to go. Questions about where, who or when would use a question word with 「か」 instead.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「ゆいさんがどこに住んでいる ___ しっていますか。」 ('Do you know where Yui lives?')?
questions.explanation: A question placed inside a sentence ends in 「か」: 「どこに住んでいるか」 is 'where she lives'. 「と」 would quote a statement, and 「を」 or 「が」 cannot follow a clause with a question word like this.

questions.stem: Arriving in Tokyo, you tell your host family 「日本ははじめてです。」 What do you mean?
options: I am going to Japan for a start.
This is my first time in Japan.
I came to Japan first of all.
Japan was the first country I chose.
questions.explanation: 「Noun ははじめてです」 says this is your first experience of something: your first time in Japan. It is a natural opening when meeting a host family.

questions.stem: What does 「子どものころ、よく川であそびました。」 mean?
options: Children often played in the river near here.
After I had children, we played by the river.
When I was a child, I often played in the river.
I often take my children to play in the river.
questions.explanation: 「Noun のころ」 means 'around the time of', so 「子どものころ」 is 'when I was a child', and the past tense 「あそびました」 confirms it is the speaker's own childhood.

questions.stem: How do you turn 「長い」 into a noun meaning 'length'?
questions.explanation: Replacing the final 「い」 of an い-adjective with 「さ」 gives a noun of measure: 「長さ」, 'length', as in 「川の長さ」. 「長く」 is the adverb form, and 「長いの」 means 'the long one'.

questions.stem: A classmate asks 「駅までどうやって行きますか。」 Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: 「どうやって」 asks how, meaning by what method, so the answer names a way of getting there: by bus. How long it takes would answer 「どのくらいかかりますか」, and when would answer 「いつ」.

questions.stem: How do you say 'two thirds' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Japanese fractions name the whole first: 「三分の二」 is 'of three parts, two'. 「二分の三」 reverses this and means three halves, a common slip for English speakers who say the top number first.

questions.stem: What is 「十万円」 in figures?
questions.explanation: Japanese counts large numbers in units of ten thousand (「万」), so 「十万」 is ten ten-thousands: 100,000. 10,000 yen is 「一万円」 and 1,000 yen is 「千円」.

questions.stem: In which year did the 「令和」 era begin?
questions.explanation: 「令和」 began on 1 May 2019, when a new emperor came to the throne, so 2019 is 令和元年, the first year of the era. 1989 is when 「平成」 began.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「おかねが ___、こまりました。」 ('I had no money, which was a problem')?
questions.explanation: 「なくて」 links a negative cause to its result: having no money caused the trouble. 「ないで」 means 'without doing' or makes a request (「わすれないで」), so it cannot give a reason here.

questions.stem: Which sentence asks a friend to help you for a moment?
options: 「ちょっとてつだってもらいませんか。」
「ちょっとてつだいませんでしたか。」
「ちょっとてつだってくれませんか。」
「ちょっとてつだってあげませんか。」
questions.explanation: 「Verb て + くれませんか」 asks someone to do something for you: 'Could you help me for a moment?' 「てあげる」 is for favours you do for others, and 「てもらいませんか」 suggests getting someone else to help rather than asking the listener.
